label: Homotopy and the Fundamental Group
notes: This chapter, spanning printed pages 183 to 216, builds the first serious algebraic invariant of a topological space. We start from continuous deformation of maps, sharpen to path homotopy fixing endpoints, and assemble loop classes into the fundamental group, the gateway to all of algebraic topology.

label: Homotopy of Maps
notes: A homotopy is a single continuous map on the product with the unit interval, not a loose sequence of pictures. The time coordinate sweeps one map continuously into another. We verify reflexivity, symmetry by reversing time, and transitivity by gluing two homotopies along a shared middle slice.

label: Path Homotopy rel Endpoints
notes: Path homotopy adds two boundary conditions to the homotopy square: the left edge stays at the initial point and the right edge at the terminal point for all time. The codomain matters, since deleting a point can destroy a deformation that was valid in the whole plane, a recurring warning.

label: Product of Paths
notes: Concatenation runs the first path at double speed, then the second, gluing where the terminal point meets the initial point. The gluing lemma supplies continuity. This representative-level product is the raw material whose homotopy classes will satisfy the group axioms after we quotient out reparametrization.

label: The Fundamental Group
notes: Fixing a base point, we take loops, identify path-homotopic ones, and multiply classes by concatenation. The resulting set of classes under this product is the fundamental group. It records how loops fail to contract, turning continuous topology into a computable algebraic group attached to the pointed space.

label: Verifying the Group Axioms
notes: Products of paths are not literally associative because the bracketings spend different fractions of the interval on each piece. Lemma 7.9 says reparametrization preserves path class, so associativity holds after quotienting. The constant loop is the identity and the reversed path is the inverse, completing every group axiom.

label: Change of Base Point
notes: In a path-connected space, a chosen path from p to q conjugates loops to give an isomorphism between the two fundamental groups. The isomorphism depends on the chosen path, not merely on the two points, since in nonabelian groups different paths can yield different conjugations of the same loop.

label: Induced Homomorphism and Functoriality
notes: A continuous map sends loops to loops by composition, descending to an induced homomorphism on fundamental groups. Identities induce identities and composites induce composites, so pi-one is a covariant functor from pointed spaces to groups. The homomorphism property follows from a literal equality of composed concatenations.

label: Homotopy Equivalence
notes: Two spaces are homotopy equivalent when continuous maps compose, in both orders, to maps homotopic to the identities. Homotopy invariance then forces the induced maps on fundamental groups to be isomorphisms, with base-point corrections supplied by the path that the homotopy traces between the two image base points.

label: Deformation Retraction of the Punctured Plane
notes: The radial homotopy slides each nonzero point straight to the unit circle while fixing points already on the circle and never crossing the origin. This strong deformation retraction exhibits the inclusion of the circle and the radial map as homotopy inverses, so the punctured plane and the circle share a fundamental group.

label: Simply Connected and Contractible Spaces
notes: A space is simply connected when it is path-connected with trivial fundamental group, and contractible when its identity map is homotopic to a constant. Spheres of dimension at least two are simply connected, proved by subdividing a loop finely, nudging it off a point, and projecting stereographically.

label: Synthesis: pi-one as a Functor
notes: We assembled homotopy, path classes, the group law, base-point change, induced homomorphisms, and homotopy equivalence into one categorical picture. The fundamental group is a covariant functor from pointed spaces to groups, and products of spaces map to products of groups, modeling the torus as the integer lattice squared.
